headline: Milford's Van Berloh argues retirement fundamentally flips accumulation-phase investing rules, with dollar-cost averaging becoming 'dollar-cost ravaging' in drawdown mode
reasoning: Van Berloh argues that all the core principles advisors rely on during accumulation — dollar-cost averaging, riding out volatility, taking risk for upside — work against retirees. In retirement, investors are withdrawing rather than adding, so a market drawdown early in retirement can permanently deplete the capital base with no time to recover. He cites research suggesting advisors need to begin repositioning portfolios 15–20 years before retirement, far earlier than the conventional 5–10 year rule of thumb. The focus shifts from return maximisation to downside protection, with metrics like Sortino ratio and max drawdown becoming more relevant than Sharpe ratio or simple return figures.
quote: Where dollar cost averaging is your friend, it is your foe in retirement because you're no longer adding, you're withdrawing. Things like we can remain invested and weather the ups and downs. Well, that doesn't work in retirement. You cannot weather the ups and downs like you can in accumulation mode because you simply don't have the time any longer. Nor can you take risk and risk large drawdowns in retirement for the potential upside that you can in accumulation because that has a fundamental impact on your ability to retire with any confidence. You simply just don't have the time to recoup that any longer.
episode_title: Dollar Cost Ravaging: Why retirement flips the rules of investing

Watkins argues bonds now carry genuine defensive characteristics unlike in 2022 when starting rates were near zero, because a growth slowdown would prompt rate cuts that would benefit bond prices. The high starting yield also means investors need equities to beat 7% to justify the additional risk, raising the bar considerably. PIMCO's base case is slowing growth but no recession, with stable rates and elevated volatility.
quote: I think what I would do is return to the base level of income is doing the work and the defensive characteristics as bond. Those bonds, those are the two things that I think really are anchoring the argument as to why now for investors... depending on your investment time horizon, you could look at something like the exchange traded fund earn that PIMCO has... That at the moment has a yield to maturity of 4.82%... we have the PAUS, which is our Australian Bond Fund, that has a yield which is a little over 6%... we have also listed on the stock exchange our PGBF exchange traded fund... And that at the moment has a yield to maturity of over 7%... your view on equities or any higher risk category needs to be that it can substantially beat 7%. And if you can't get comfortable that something's going to substantially beat 7%, then bonds are a pretty compelling place to be putting money today.
episode_title: Where Bonds Go, Stocks Follow with Sam Watkins

headline: Earnings season showing uneven results with brutal market reactions to misses or soft outlooks, particularly for AI-related stocks

headline: PIMCO sees disconnect between rising bond yields and surging equity markets, driven by AI euphoria masking valuation pressure
reasoning: Rising interest rates create a gravitational pull on equity valuations by increasing the discount rate applied to future earnings, making them worth less in present value terms. Despite this, the US equity market has had eight consecutive winning weeks and continues making all-time highs. Watkins attributes this to AI euphoria, with unbelievable growth expectations priced into AI-exposed stocks and margin improvement expectations for others. He acknowledges the partial argument that future earnings may have risen enough to offset higher discount rates but views the AI benefit as uncertain in timing and distribution.
quote: What Warren Buffett was really getting at there is that the fundamental value of assets is priced from a risk-free rate concept... The higher that interest rate where a person could with little to no risk get a return, the more that other assets that are further out that risk spectrum need to work... when you look at a fundamental value of a stock, what it is is simply expectation of forward earnings discounted to today's price. Those forward earnings, when you discount them back at a higher interest rate, are simply worth less today. When you see interest rates move higher, it does put a gravitational pull on equity prices... I think the biggest thing that's driving markets at the moment is really the euphoria around AI.
episode_title: Where Bonds Go, Stocks Follow with Sam Watkins

headline: Charlie Viola says investment property fundamentals still matter more than tax benefits, and negative gearing changes should not override asset quality decisions
reasoning: Viola notes that negative gearing proposals may boost demand for new off-the-plan properties but warns investors should prioritise fundamental drivers: proximity to amenities, low holding costs, and favourable supply/demand dynamics. He cautions that negative gearing is literally negative — spending a dollar to save 50 cents — and investors must account for cumulative losses when calculating true IRR. The leverage benefit remains powerful for wealth accumulators with good incomes, but the asset itself must be expected to produce a substantial capital gain to justify the strategy.
quote: We still think that if you're buying a property for investment purposes, and you want it to have long-term growth, there are some normal fundamentals that go with that. And we don't think that's changed... What people seem to forget about negative gearing is that it's negative. So you're literally spending a dollar to save 50 cents... At the other end, when you sell it, you need to have a great big positive to obviously have offset all of the losses that you've made along the way. So people need to take that into account. But the leverage is powerful and especially people who have got reasonably good incomes and ability to also invest around that, it still makes sense to do.
